source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 fell for the Linda conjunction fallacy like people. It did not fall for the cab-problem base-rate error.
numbers: Linda: chose option 2 (bank teller and feminist). Cab problem: answered about correct, unlike people. All 3 CRT items: intuitive wrong answer.
limits: Early model (GPT-3 davinci era); single vignettes, not large samples. Stimuli might be memorised.
agent_relevance: Famous vignettes may be recalled from training, so success or failure on them is weak evidence. Use fresh item variants.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 showed framing effect, certainty effect and overweighting of small probability differences. Three other Kahneman-Tversky biases were not found.
numbers: Overweighting: a 1% vs 2% gap weighed more than a 41% vs 42% gap. Three of six biases absent.
limits: Choices from descriptions; one model; no chain of thought.
agent_relevance: Prospect-theory style distortions can appear in model choices, so risky-choice steps need a check against expected value.

source: Binz and Schulz (2022) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: Small perturbations to well-known tasks sent GPT-3 astray. It looked like pattern recall, not rule use.
numbers: Cab task with colour changed to black: answered 20%. CRT with the premise changed: still said 10 cents. Reverse Wason failed.
quote: Small perturbations to vignette-based tasks can lead GPT-3 vastly astray
limits: Perturbation set is small and hand-made.
agent_relevance: Test the scaffold on perturbed variants, not on the classic wording.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models (CRT and semantic illusions)
finding: Older GPT-3 models gave the human-like intuitive wrong answer on CRT. Newer ChatGPT and GPT-4 stopped doing so and became hyperrational.
numbers: Correct responses: davinci-003 5%, humans 38%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, ChatGPT-4 96%. Intuitive wrong: davinci-003 80%, humans 55%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, GPT-4 0%. Babbage under 5% intuitive, curie 21%.
limits: CRT items are widely published, so contamination is possible. Human baseline from earlier studies (n=3,428 for CRT).
agent_relevance: The classic bias set is mostly solved in frontier models. It is a weak test of a scaffold; use novel or perturbed items.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models (CRT and semantic illusions)
finding: Chain-of-thought prompting cut intuitive errors in an older model. Blocking chain of thought barely hurt the newest model.
numbers: davinci-003 with CoT: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29%. Blocking CoT: GPT-4 correct 95% to 88%, intuitive 0% to 10%; ChatGPT-3.5 correct unchanged (p=.49).
limits: One task family. Prompt told models to answer without reasoning.
agent_relevance: Scaffold gain from a System-2 step is large for weak models and small for strong ones. Measure per model.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models (CRT and semantic illusions)
finding: A few worked examples fixed the CRT trap in an older model.
numbers: Type 1 tasks: correct 2% to 92% after two examples. Another type: 12% to 92% after seven examples.
limits: Same task type as the examples, so it may teach the pattern not the principle.
agent_relevance: Worked examples of debiased solutions work in-distribution; check transfer to new task types.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee and Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) showed anchoring, with estimates pulled toward random anchors, close to humans.
numbers: Low anchor mean 20.83 (ChatGPT) vs 22.50 (humans). High anchor 105.97 vs 80.50. ChatGPT low vs high: t(58)=8.78, p<.0001. GPT-4 in 5 trials: 22.0 low, 94.33 high.
limits: Small samples (about 30 each); GPT-4 only 5 trials per condition. Conflicts with Shaki et al., who found no anchoring in GPT-3.
agent_relevance: Model anchors on any number in the prompt, even random ones. Keep irrelevant numbers out of prompts and tool outputs.

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee and Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT showed the conjunction fallacy on a new item and was swayed by salient anecdotes. Humans did too.
numbers: Conjunction item: ChatGPT picked the conjunction 18 of 20 times; 10 human participants picked the conjunction and 10 picked the single event. Framing: positive-frame efficacy 5.2 vs negative-frame 4.6, significant.
limits: Novel prompts but tiny n; justifications were similar to humans, which the authors tie to language.
agent_relevance: Representativeness-style errors can be produced by text patterns alone, so an agent may need an explicit probability-check step.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld and Belinkov (2024) Instructed to bias: instruction-tuned LMs exhibit emergent cognitive bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF made decoy, certainty and belief biases stronger in GPT-3, Mistral and T5 families.
numbers: Bias score = treatment minus control choice rate. Instruction-tuned models (Flan-T5, Mistral-Instruct, GPT-4) had higher scores than base models on most biases.
limits: Some base-model scores were negative because of positional choice of the last option, not value-based choice.
agent_relevance: Aligned chat models can be more biased than raw ones in some cases. Do not assume tuning removes heuristics.

source: Itzhak, Stanovsky, Rosenfeld and Belinkov (2024) Instructed to bias: instruction-tuned LMs exhibit emergent cognitive bias
finding: Bias grows with model size for several biases, and 1-shot prompting did not remove it in GPT-4.
numbers: Table 4: GPT-4 vs DaVinci-003 in 1-shot; decoy-expensive score 0.38 for GPT-4 vs 0.00 for DaVinci; certainty and belief scores significant for both.
limits: Scores in a -1 to 1 range; one prompt wording family.
agent_relevance: Scale does not fix it; test the actual deployed model.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of LLMs via human cognitive biases
finding: Using framing, anchoring and availability as hypotheses, they found Codex and CodeGen fail predictably in code generation.
numbers: Irrelevant preceding function plus a framing line: Codex functional accuracy 32.9% to 2.4-10.6%; Codex output the framing line 62.2-92.7% of the time. CodeGen 25.6% to 1.5-11.0%.
quote: Codex errs predictably based on how the input prompt is framed, adjusts outputs towards anchors
limits: HumanEval; davinci-001 Codex and CodeGen; old models.
agent_relevance: Context in an agent loop (earlier code, earlier answers) acts as an anchor. Clean the context before each step.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing failures of LLMs via human cognitive biases
finding: Anchor functions containing a bug lowered accuracy, and parts of the bug leaked into the solution. The same method found a high-impact error, deleting files.
numbers: Anchor lines were print-var and add-var variants; accuracy fell versus no-anchor baseline (shown in figures only; exact values not recorded).
limits: Exact accuracy drops from the figure were not read.
agent_relevance: Cognitive-bias hypotheses are a cheap way to design red-team tests for an agent.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models
finding: Seven LLMs on classic reasoning tasks were irrational, but mostly not in the human-biased way. Wrong answers often did not match known human biases.
numbers: Correct with sound reasoning: GPT-4 0.692, Claude 2 0.550, Bard 0.358, GPT-3.5 0.292, Llama-2-70b 0.150, 13b 0.050, 7b 0.025. Incorrect and non-human-like: Llama-2-13b 0.700, 7b 0.608, GPT-3.5 0.408, GPT-4 0.142. Incorrect human-like: GPT-3.5 0.217, Llama-2-7b 0.167, GPT-4 0.042.
limits: Small battery (Wason, Linda, Monty Hall and similar); responses coded by hand; Llama-2-70b gave no answer 0.417.
agent_relevance: Model errors are not just human heuristics. A debiasing step aimed at human bias lists will miss many errors.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in large language models
finding: The same prompt gave very different answers across runs: a second kind of irrationality that humans do not show in the same way.
numbers: Same model gave correct reasoning in some runs and illogical reasoning in others; example Llama-2-7b on Monty Hall said switching does not matter.
limits: Sampling temperature effect not isolated.
agent_relevance: Sample several times and use a consistency check (agreement) before trusting one answer.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: BiasBuster tested anchoring, framing, status quo, primacy and group attribution in student-admission decisions. Prompt-induced biases appeared in all models.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under the reject framing. Llama-2 7B classed 32.1% fewer females as good at math. No clear human-like status quo bias.
limits: Synthetic admission task; models differ strongly in which bias they show.
agent_relevance: Framing of the question (admit vs reject) changes decisions. Ask both frames and compare.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Awareness prompts gave small gains. Few-shot debiasing sometimes broke the model (all admit or all reject). Letting the model rewrite its own prompt (self-help) worked best.
numbers: Few-shot failures: admission or rejection ratio under 1%. Self-help left 0% (Llama-2 13B) and 1.4% (Llama-2 7B) biased framing prompts; group attribution 0%; status quo 6% for one Llama model.
limits: Cross-model table not fully read; contrastive prompts reached delta near 1.0 only by failing to follow instructions.
agent_relevance: Prompt rewriting by the model itself is a cheap debias step; test that it does not cause collapse to one answer.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-adaptive cognitive debiasing (SACD) for LLMs in decision-making
finding: SACD loops three steps: find the bias, analyse it, rewrite the prompt. It gave the lowest bias scores in single and multi-bias prompts across finance, health and law.
numbers: Avg bias scores: FOMC 0.0300-0.1570 vs best baseline 0.0625-0.3490; PubMedQA 0.0425-0.1790 vs 0.0725-0.4175; LegalBench 0.0400-0.1235 vs 0.0725-0.2625. Four LLMs.
limits: Bias score is a treatment vs control gap, so it measures sensitivity, not accuracy; benchmarks are classification tasks.
agent_relevance: A bias-check-and-rewrite loop is a direct candidate for an operator in the schema.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-adaptive cognitive debiasing (SACD) for LLMs in decision-making
finding: Chain of thought helped a little. Reflexion and multi-agent debate had the highest bias scores and amplified bias.
numbers: CoT avg bias 0.2470-0.6150 across domains. Multi-agent debate 0.5155 on FOMC with gpt-3.5-turbo. Reflexion 0.5585 on PubMedQA with llama3.1-70b.
quote: Reflexion and Multi-agent debate methods consistently exhibit the highest bias scores
limits: Authors explain amplification as learning from biased feedback; not tested separately.
agent_relevance: Reflection and debate loops can reinforce a bias present in the prompt. Remove the biased cue before the loop, not only after.

source: Zhong et al. (2025) Balancing rigor and utility: mitigating cognitive biases in LLMs for multiple-choice questions
finding: Telling the model to inspect the question for bias traps, and letting it abstain, raised accuracy on bias-trap multiple choice.
numbers: Accuracy GPT-4: standard 33.2, general bias inspection 68.3, specific bias inspection 79.0 (no abstain); with abstain 48.4, 73.8, 93.5. Gemini 1.0 Pro 44.4 to 80.0. LLaMA3-70B 22.4 to 50.2.
limits: Custom BRU dataset; abstention is never a correct answer so accuracy is on valid votes.
agent_relevance: Name the likely bias trap and allow I-do-not-know. Gains are large on trap items; unknown on ordinary items.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring bias in large language models: an experimental study
finding: GPT-4 and GPT-4o were pulled by numeric hints. Chain of thought, thoughts-of-principles, ignore-anchor and reflection prompts did not fix it.
numbers: p-values per question under each strategy tabled; none reliably removed the effect. Giving both a high and a low hint (Both-Anchor) brought GPT-4 answers close to the bias-free value.
quote: one needs to collect hints from comprehensive angles
limits: School-level study, small question set.
agent_relevance: Collect evidence from several angles so no single cue dominates; do not rely on a say-ignore-it instruction.

source: Malberg et al. (2025) A comprehensive evaluation of cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: Largest test so far: 30 cognitive biases, 20 LLMs, 30,000 generated tests. All 30 biases showed up in at least some models.
numbers: Only Status-Quo Bias and Disposition Effect had strongly negative mean scores. Smallest model (Llama 1B) looked least biased but failed to decide in 33% of tests. Random baseline showed no bias.
limits: Tests are LLM-generated managerial scenarios; bias score assumes a treatment-minus-control design.
agent_relevance: Low bias score can hide low competence; pair bias tests with decision-failure rate.

source: Koo et al. (2024) Benchmarking cognitive biases in LLMs as evaluators (CoBBLEr)
finding: 16 LLMs used as judges showed order, compassion fade, egocentric, salience, bandwagon and attentional biases. About 40% of comparisons showed a bias.
numbers: About 42K samples per bias per model (630K total). Order bias in 11 of 15 models. Bandwagon: over 70% of evaluations followed a fake 85%-preferred statistic. Salience (length) proportion 0.56 GPT-4, 0.63 ChatGPT, 0.62 Llama-2.
limits: Human preference set is 6 annotators and 300 annotations; weak models may fail the format.
agent_relevance: An LLM judge or critic step inside an agent is biased: shuffle order, hide authorship, ignore popularity claims.

source: Takenami et al. (2025) How does cognitive bias affect LLMs? Anchoring in price negotiation simulations
finding: Seller LLM agents using an anchor got better prices from buyer LLMs, like humans. Reasoning models reduced the effect.
numbers: o1 mitigated the anchoring effect in 35 of 50 matched cases versus GPT-4o. QwQ beat its base Qwen2.5 even without being told about the anchor. Telling the buyer about the anchor reduced the cost but did not remove the effect.
limits: Simulated negotiations; no personality trait correlated significantly with susceptibility.
agent_relevance: Extended deliberation helps anchoring; awareness alone does not (matches human findings).

source: Huang et al. (2026) Understanding the anchoring effect of LLM with synthetic data (SynAnchors)
finding: Anchoring appears in many LLMs, acts in shallow layers, and conventional mitigations fail. Reasoning helps most but does not remove it.
numbers: 22% to 61% of questions anchored across models. Reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3 thinking) had the lowest ratios; traces that mention the anchor correlate with less bias.
limits: Dataset designed to avoid memorised items; ratio columns in the table not fully mapped.
agent_relevance: Make the model state and discount the anchor in its reasoning trace.

source: Valencia-Clavijo (2026) Anchors in the machine: behavioral and attributional evidence of anchoring bias in LLMs
finding: Log-probability tests across six open models show mostly positive anchoring, varying widely. Behaviour and input attribution do not always agree.
numbers: Highest Anchoring Bias Sensitivity Score: Gemma-2B, Phi-2, Llama-2-7B. Exact Banzhaf attribution over prompt fields.
limits: Small open models only; positive control used to reduce memorisation.
agent_relevance: Behavioural bias does not prove the anchor field caused it; use attribution checks before trusting a debias fix.

source: Shaki, Kraus and Wooldridge (2023) Cognitive effects in large language models
finding: GPT-3 showed priming, distance, SNARC and size congruity effects, but not anchoring. This disagrees with Suri et al. on GPT-3.5.
numbers: Anchoring table: small vs large anchor estimates differed by only a few units (for example 45.78 vs 42.04 in one case) and not in the human direction.
limits: Different model (GPT-3 vs GPT-3.5), different prompts; authors ask whether effects are imitated or reinvented.
agent_relevance: Anchoring results depend on prompt format and model version; replicate on the target model.

source: Shahriar et al. (2026) Words speak louder than code: cognitive heuristics in LLM-based code vulnerability detection
finding: Eight LLMs judging code for vulnerabilities were swayed by halo (author), framing (task goal) and anchoring (earlier analysis) cues while the code was fixed.
numbers: Mean relative recall gap: framing 33.2%, anchoring 23.5%, halo 18.4%. 43 of 48 gaps significant in C/C++, 44 of 48 Java, 46 of 48 Python. Anchoring raised recall 11.16 points on reasoning-dependent bugs vs 4.24 on pattern ones.
limits: Zero-shot function-level; PrimeVul; underlying cause of inverse susceptibility unexplained.
agent_relevance: Metadata and earlier verdicts in an agent context bias later judgements. Strip them before an independent verification step.

source: Shahriar et al. (2026) Words speak louder than code: cognitive heuristics in LLM-based code vulnerability detection
finding: Combining the three cues beat single cues in most models. Prompt-only defences were weak and backfired on Claude.
numbers: Combined attack success: Mistral nearly 75% (best single under 51%), Gemini 45% (best single 25%). Strong defence: all open models still above 39% success; four models above 80% under the weak defence; counterproductive on Claude.
quote: prompt-based defenses are insufficient against cognitive attacks
limits: Attack success counts only flips from correct vulnerable verdicts.
agent_relevance: An ignore-the-context instruction is not a debias method; remove the cue or use independent passes.

source: Hagendorff et al. (2024) Machine psychology
finding: Review arguing that psychology experiments on LLMs reveal behaviour beyond benchmarks and listing caveats of transferring human methods to machines.
numbers: No numbers recorded; only the abstract text was read in the PDF.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Supports paradigm-style tests with prompt variants and repeated sampling for agent evaluation.
